catalog_citation: Noonan, Michael. 2003. Recent language contact in the Nepal Himalaya. In David Bradley, Randy LaPolla, Boyd Michailovsky & Graham Thurgood (eds.), Language variation: papers on variation and change in the Sinosphere and in the Indosphere in honour of James A. Matisoff, 65-87. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. [author's preprint]
catalog_locator: preprint p. 7 'Stress'; Table 2 Part 2 p. 19 row 'stress' S.Magar +T/-N and legend; Table 1 p. 16 row 'stress' Himalayish = 'relatively weak, word boundary stress: on root'
catalog_quote: In the Bodic groupings in our sample, stress was predictable and was generally fixed on the root. Where languages have borrowed large amounts of Nepali vocabulary, they have accommodated to the Nepali stress pattern. … Kham: T.Magar: S.Magar: … stress +T/-N +T/-N +T/-N +T/-N +T/-N … +T/-N = consistent with the structural profile of the grouping and not consonant with Nepali
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

tone_statements.citation: Noonan, Michael. 2003. Recent language contact in the Nepal Himalaya. In David Bradley, Randy LaPolla, Boyd Michailovsky & Graham Thurgood (eds.), Language variation: papers on variation and change in the Sinosphere and in the Indosphere in honour of James A. Matisoff, 65-87. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. [author's preprint, 25 pp., open via Internet Archive copy of www.uwm.edu/~noonan/Recent Language ]
tone_statements.quote: Chantyal has lost its tone system under Nepali — and perhaps Magar — influ- ence. It retains an opposition of murmured vs plain syllabic nuclei, which resembles that found in some Magar dialects. Of the Himalayish languages in our sample, only Kham has acquired a tone sys- tem, almost certainly under Bodish influence. [...] The two Magar dialects have mumur in more- or-less the Nepali fashion, though Tanahu shows signs of a ‘register’ system similar to that which Chantyal must have had after losing its tone system.
tone_statements.locator: author's preprint pp. 4-5, section 'phonological features' paragraphs 'Tone' and 'Murmur'; cf. table p.19 (Kham/T.Magar/S.Magar/Newari columns, row 'tone': S.Magar +T/+N)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone in Syangja (Western) Magar; contrastive murmur/breathy voice on the Nepali pattern; Tanahu (Eastern) shows incipient register.

sources.note: No Magar sketch (demographic mentions only).

sources.citation: Grierson, George A. (S. Konow). 1909. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. III Part I, 'Magari' pp. 206-211.
sources.note: 'Pronunciation' paragraph treats vowels, long vowels only in loans, consonants, aspiration; no accent/stress statement.

sources.citation: Regmi, Pratigya. 2013. Tense, aspect and modality (TAM) in the Magar Dhut [Nawalparasi]. MA thesis, Central Dept. of Linguistics, Tribhuvan University. TUCL hdl 20.500.14540/16294.
sources.note: No phonology chapter; nothing on stress. Literature review (pp.15-21) lists Nepali-medium Magar grammars/dictionaries (Magar 1993a; Thapa 2009, 2010) that give phonemic inventories.

sources.citation: Grunow-Hårsta, Karen. 2011. Adjectives and adjectivals in Magar. Himalayan Linguistics 10(1): 101-126. doi 10.5070/H910123570.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Useful for identity: western dialects = Syangja, Palpa (verb agreement, consistent ergativity); eastern = Tanahu, Gorkha, Nawalparasi (pp.101-102, fn.5-6).

sources.citation: Baskaran, S. Ganesh. 2009. Mangari. In Linguistic Survey of India: Sikkim, Part I, pp. 561-613. Kolkata: Language Division, Office of the Registrar General, India.
sources.note: Sec. 2.1.2 (p.564): 'Nasalisation is the only suprasegmental feature realized in mangari language.' No statement of stress position anywhere in the sketch (syllable section 2.5 lists syllable types only). Variety = Sikkim diaspora Magar (Glottolog files it under Eastern Magar).

sources.citation: Thapa, Bhanukumari. 2008 (2065 VS). Dailekhma boline Magar Dhut bhasako adhyayan [A study of the Magar Dhut language spoken in Dailekh]. MA thesis (Nepali medium, Preeti-font), Tribhuvan University. TUCL hdl 20.500.14540/8133.
sources.note: Chapter 2 (dhvani/varna vyavastha) gives 32 consonants and 12 vowels with minimal pairs and articulatory classification; no section on balaghat (stress), sur (tone) or any suprasegmental. Silent.

sources.citation: Grunow-Hårsta, Karen. 2007. Evidentiality and mirativity in Magar. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 30(2): 151-194.
sources.note: Nothing on stress (morphosyntax only).

sources.citation: Hale, Austin (ed.). 1973. Clause, sentence, and discourse patterns in selected languages of Nepal, Part IV: Word lists. SIL Publications in Linguistics 40(4). Introduction sec. E 'Magar', pp. 18-19 (analysis after Shepherd & Shepherd 1971; Yanchok, Tanahu District).

sources.note: Phoneme chart; 'Length is not contrastive for Magar vowels'; breathiness treated as a syllable feature with concomitant pitch lowering. No stress statement. Dialect is Yanchok near Bandipur, Tanahu = Eastern Magar.

sources.citation: WALS Online (Dryer & Haspelmath eds.), CLDF copy: languages mag 'Magar' (source Shepherd & Shepherd 1973) and msy 'Magar (Syangja)' (source Noonan 2003).
sources.note: No values for stress features 14A-17A (Goedemans & van der Hulst) for either Magar entry; StressTyp-type second-hand coding therefore absent.

sources.citation: Subba, Subhadra. 1972. Descriptive analysis of Magar: a Tibeto-Burman language. PhD thesis, Deccan College / University of Poona (guide A.R. Kelkar). x+255 pp. [Shodhganga hdl 10603/155073; image-only scan, scanned here]
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Ch.1 Phonology sec. 1.1.2 (p.3): 'Tone contrasts were not detected in Magar.' with the author's handwritten addendum 'No study was made of accent and intonation in Magar.' Syllable section (1.4, pp.24-30) treats division/types only. Explicitly silent on stress placement. NB principal informant from Rising, Tanahu (eastern dialect); secondary informants from Syaju (Palpa) and Rahu (Syangja) = western dialects (Intro p. viii).
